Membership
MEM-bur-ship
noun (ecclesiastical)
From Latin membrum, a limb or part of a body; covenantal belonging to a particular local church as a member of Christ's body.

📖 Biblical Definition

Church membership is the covenantal belonging of a professing believer to a particular local church, by which he is knit to a body, submits to its elders, and takes up his place among the saints. The New Testament knows no Christian who floats unattached. The Lord adds the saved to the church (Acts 2:47), Paul writes to defined congregations whose members are counted and known, and the metaphor of the body assumes that each member has a fixed place, a function, and a mutual obligation to the rest. Membership is therefore not an institutional formality but the visible form of love and accountability: the believer pledges himself to a people, and the elders take responsibility for his soul. Hebrews 13:17 commands obedience and submission to those who watch over souls as men who must give account—a charge meaningless apart from a recognized flock. Through membership the church admits a credible profession of faith, ordinarily sealed in baptism, and receives the believer to the Lord's table, to discipline, and to the ordinary means of grace. It binds him to attendance, to giving, to the use of his gifts, and to bearing the burdens of others. Far from cramping liberty, membership is the structure of Christian belonging—the named, accountable, affectionate union of a saint to a congregation under Christ the Head, where he is loved, watched, corrected, and built up toward maturity in the faith.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Membership is the covenantal joining of a believer to a particular local church under the oversight of its elders.

expand to see more

MEMBERSHIP, noun. From Latin membrum, a limb or part of a body.

The state of being a member; belonging as a constituent part of a whole.

In the church, the covenantal union of a professing believer to a particular congregation.

The body of members collectively: "the whole membership assembled."

Scripture grounds it: "So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another" (Romans 12:5).

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 12:5 — "So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another."

1Co 12:27 — "Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular."

Act 2:47 — "Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved."

Heb 13:17 — "Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Modern individualism redefines faith as a private affair needing no commitment to a local body.

expand to see more

The age treats church membership as optional—a consumer's convenience he may take up, set down, or skip entirely, as though Christ saves isolated souls who owe nothing to a people. The believer is told he can love Jesus without joining a church, attend anonymously, give nothing, submit to no one, and remain unknown. This is not the religion of the New Testament. There the saved are added to the church, counted, named, watched over, and held to account. The unattached Christian is a contradiction the apostles never imagined.

The recovery is to see membership as covenant, not contract—a binding of love by which a believer says to a particular people, you are mine and I am yours under Christ. Hebrews 13:17 will not let the soul wander un-shepherded; it puts him under men who must give account for him. To reclaim membership is to reclaim accountability, mutual burden-bearing, and the visible body of Christ against the corrosive lie that faith is a solitary transaction between the individual and God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on the body metaphor and the apostolic practice of receiving believers into defined congregations.

expand to see more

Romans 12:5 makes believers members one of another in one body.

1 Corinthians 12:27 names the saints the body of Christ, members in particular.

Acts 2:47 records the Lord adding the saved to the church.

Hebrews 13:17 binds members to obey and submit to those who watch over their souls.

The 1689 Confession ties members to a particular church by mutual consent and discipline.

Usage

"Used of formal belonging: "he applied for membership at the congregation.""

"Used of the body of members together: "the membership voted to call a pastor.""

"Used of the duties entailed: "membership means submission to the elders.""
